l: Heman, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: Heman is called the king's seer in the words of God, to lift up the horn. God gave him fourteen sons, who are named, and three daughters, and his sons served under his hands in song in the LORD's house under the king's order.

l: musicians' service, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: The service was prophesying with harps, stringed instruments, and cymbals, for song in the LORD's house and the service of God's house. It was organized under Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman, who were under the king's order.

l: musicians (the instructed singers), 1 Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: The singers, together with their brothers who were instructed in singing to the LORD and were skillful, numbered two hundred eighty-eight. They were all included in the casting of lots for their offices.

l: casting of lots, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: The musicians cast lots for their offices, all alike, small and great, teacher and student. The lots determined the order of the twenty-four divisions, beginning with Joseph of Asaph's house.

l: twenty-four divisions, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 25
s: The lots produced twenty-four divisions, each consisting of the named leader with his sons and brothers, twelve in each. They ran from the first lot, to Joseph, to the twenty-fourth, to Romamti-Ezer.

l: 1 Chronicles, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: Chapter 26 lists the Levitical doorkeepers and treasurers of David's organization. The doorkeeper divisions come from the Korahites (Meshelemiah, Obed-Edom) and from Merari (Hosah), and lots were cast by fathers' houses to assign each gate: east, north, south, west and the storehouse. Other Levites were put over the treasuries of God's house and the dedicated things, with Shelomoth and his brothers in charge of the dedicated gifts given by David, Samuel, Saul, Abner, Joab and others. The chapter closes with Chenaniah, Hashabiah and Jerijah of the Izharites and Hebronites, who were appointed as officers, judges and overseers for Israel on both sides of the Jordan, in matters of the LORD and the king.

l: Meshelemiah, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: Meshelemiah, a Korahite of the sons of Asaph, had seven sons, beginning with Zechariah the firstborn. He and his sons and brothers numbered eighteen valiant men among the doorkeepers.

l: Obed-Edom, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: Obed-Edom had eight sons, and the text says God blessed him. With his sons and relatives, sixty-two able men served as doorkeepers, and the lot gave him the south gate and his sons the storehouse.

l: Hosah, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: Hosah, of the children of Merari, had sons Shimri, whom his father made chief though not firstborn, Hilkiah, Tebaliah and Zechariah, thirteen sons and brothers in all. With Shuppim he received the west lot by the gate of Shallecheth at the ascending causeway.

l: doorkeepers, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: The doorkeepers were organized in divisions drawn from the Korahites and the sons of Merari, with chief men serving like their brothers in the LORD's house. Guards were assigned by gate: six on the east, four a day on the north and south, two and two at the storehouse, and four at the causeway plus two at Parbar on the west.

l: lot casting, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: Lots were cast, small and great alike, by fathers' houses to assign each gate. The east fell to Shelemiah, the north to his son Zechariah the wise counselor, the south to Obed-Edom, with the storehouse to his sons, and the west to Shuppim and Hosah.

l: LORD's house, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: The doorkeepers ministered in the LORD's house and guarded its gates and storehouse. Its treasures were overseen by Jehieli's sons Zetham and Joel, and plunder from battles was dedicated to repair it.

l: treasuries, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: Ahijah was over the treasures of God's house, and Zetham and Joel, sons of Jehieli the Gershonite, were over the treasures of the LORD's house. Shebuel son of Gershom, son of Moses, was ruler over the treasuries.

l: Shelomoth, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: Shelomoth, a descendant of Eliezer through Rehabiah, Jeshaiah, Joram and Zichri, was over all the treasuries of the dedicated things together with his brothers. Everything dedicated by David, the captains, Samuel, Saul, Abner, Joab and others was under his hand.

l: dedicated things, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: The dedicated things were given by King David, the heads of fathers' households, the army captains, and earlier figures such as Samuel, Saul, Abner and Joab. Some came from plunder won in battles to repair the LORD's house, and Shelomoth and his brothers kept them.

l: Hashabiah, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: Hashabiah, a Hebronite, and his brothers, 1,700 men of valor, had oversight of Israel west of the Jordan for all the business of the LORD and the service of the king.

l: Jerijah, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 26
s: Jerijah was chief of the Hebronites by their generations and fathers' households. In the fortieth year of David's reign they were sought out, and mighty men of valor were found among them at Jazer of Gilead.

l: 1 Chronicles, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 27
s: Chapter 27 lists the organization of Israel's king David's administration. Twelve army divisions of twenty-four thousand each served month by month, each under a named captain such as Jashobeam, Dodai, Benaiah, and Asahel. The chapter also names a ruler over each tribe of Israel, notes that David did not count those twenty and under and that Joab's unfinished census brought wrath on Israel and was not recorded in the chronicles. It then lists officials over King David's treasures, fields, vineyards, trees, herds, camels, donkeys, and flocks, and closes with David's counselors Jonathan, Jehiel, Ahithophel, Hushai, Jehoiada, and Abiathar, with Joab as captain of the army.

l: David, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 27
s: David is the king whose service structure is described: divisions serve him month by month, and officials manage his property. He did not take the number of those twenty years old and under because the LORD had said he would increase Israel like the stars of the sky, and the census Joab began was not entered in his chronicles. He also has counselors and a friend, including Ahithophel and Hushai.

l: Israel, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 27
s: Israel is organized into divisions of twenty-four thousand serving the king monthly, with rulers over its tribes. Wrath came on Israel because of Joab's unfinished census, and the LORD had said he would increase Israel like the stars of the sky.

l: Joab, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 27
s: Joab the son of Zeruiah began a census but did not finish it, and wrath came on Israel for this. He is also named as captain of the king's army, and his brother Asahel is captain of the fourth month's division.

l: census, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 27
s: Joab began a census but did not finish it, and wrath came on Israel for it. The number was not put into the account in King David's chronicles. David had also not counted those twenty and under, since the LORD had promised to increase Israel like the stars of the sky.

l: twelve monthly divisions, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 27
s: Twelve divisions of twenty-four thousand each came in and went out month by month through the year, each led by a named captain for its month. The captains run from Jashobeam for the first month to Heldai for the twelfth, and include Benaiah the son of Jehoiada for the third and Asahel the brother of Joab for the fourth.

l: tribal rulers (tribes of Israel), 1 Chronicles, Chapter 27
s: Each tribe of Israel had a named ruler, including Eliezer over the Reubenites, Zadok for Aaron, Elihu of Judah, and Azarel of Dan. Half-tribes of Manasseh had two rulers, Joel and Iddo, and the passage calls them the captains of the tribes of Israel.

l: royal property managers (David's property), 1 Chronicles, Chapter 27
s: Named officials oversaw King David's property: Azmaveth and Jonathan over the treasures, Ezri over field work, Shimei and Zabdi over vineyards and wine, Baal Hanan and Joash over olive and sycamore trees and oil, and others over herds, camels, donkeys, and flocks. The text calls them all rulers of the property which was King David's.

l: 1 Chronicles, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: David gathers all the princes, captains, rulers, officers, and mighty men of Israel at Jerusalem and addresses them. He explains that God forbade him to build the temple because he was a man of war who shed blood, and that the LORD chose Solomon to build it and to sit on the throne of the LORD's kingdom. David charges the assembly to keep the LORD's commandments and charges Solomon to serve God with a perfect heart, warning that forsaking him means being cast off forever. He gives Solomon the plans for the temple, its courts, rooms, treasuries, priestly divisions, and the weights of gold and silver for its vessels, which he says he received in writing from the LORD's hand. David then encourages Solomon to be strong and not fear, promising that God will be with him and that skilled volunteers, the priests, Levites, captains, and people will help him.

l: David, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: David assembles Israel's leaders at Jerusalem and tells them that he wished to build a house of rest for the ark but was forbidden because he was a man of war who had shed blood. He recounts that the LORD chose him as king and chose Solomon as his successor, then hands Solomon the temple plans, which he says he understood in writing from the LORD's hand. He charges Solomon to be strong and courageous and promises that God will not fail him.

l: Solomon, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: Solomon is named by David as the son the LORD has chosen out of many to sit on the throne of the LORD's kingdom and to build the LORD's house and courts. The LORD promises to be his father and to establish his kingdom forever if he keeps the commandments. David charges him to serve God with a perfect heart and a willing mind, warns him of being cast off if he forsakes God, and gives him the temple plans.

l: LORD, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: The LORD is said to have chosen David as king, Judah as prince, and Solomon to build his house and reign, promising to be Solomon's father and to establish his kingdom forever if he obeys. He forbade David to build because of bloodshed, searches all hearts and understands the thoughts, and is found by those who seek him but casts off those who forsake him. David says the LORD gave him the temple pattern in writing and that the LORD will be with Solomon until the work is finished.

l: Israel, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: Israel is the kingdom over which the LORD chose David, and then Solomon, to rule. Its assembled leaders are urged in the sight of all Israel to observe and seek out all the LORD's commandments so that they may possess the good land and leave it as an inheritance to their children forever.

l: God's house, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: The temple is to be built by Solomon rather than David, as a house for the LORD's name and a house of rest for the ark of the covenant and the footstool of God. Its porch, houses, treasuries, upper and inner rooms, place of the mercy seat, courts, and service vessels are all covered in the plans David gives. The work is to be staffed by the divisions of priests and Levites and by skilled willing workers.

l: temple plans, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: David gives Solomon the plans covering the porch, rooms, treasuries, courts, the divisions of priests and Levites, and the vessels of service. They specify gold and silver by weight for vessels, lamp stands, tables of show bread, forks, basins, cups, bowls, the altar of incense, and the chariot with the cherubim covering the ark. David says he was made to understand all the works of this pattern in writing from the LORD's hand, and some of the plans came by the Spirit.

l: princes of Israel, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 28
s: David summons the princes of the tribes, captains of divisions, thousands and hundreds, rulers over the king's possessions, officers, and mighty men to Jerusalem. They hear David explain the LORD's choice of Solomon and are charged to keep all the LORD's commandments. David also tells Solomon that the captains and all the people will be entirely at his command.

l: 1 Chronicles, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 29
s: King David tells the assembly that his young son Solomon has been chosen by God to build the temple, and he announces the gold, silver, and other materials he has prepared plus a personal gift of three thousand talents of gold and seven thousand talents of silver. The princes, tribal leaders, captains, and royal officers respond by giving large amounts of gold, silver, bronze, iron, and precious stones. David praises the LORD, acknowledges that everything comes from God, and prays that the people's hearts stay devoted and that Solomon receives a perfect heart. The assembly blesses the LORD, offers thousands of sacrifices, and makes Solomon king a second time, anointing him with Zadok as priest. The chapter closes with Solomon's rise, David's death after forty years of reign, and a note that David's acts are recorded in the histories of Samuel, Nathan, and Gad.

l: David, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 29
s: David tells the assembly that Solomon is young and the work is great, and he gives his own treasure of gold and silver in addition to all he has prepared for the house. He praises the LORD, says all things come from God, and prays that the people stay devoted and that Solomon receives a perfect heart. He dies at a good old age after reigning forty years, seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem, and Solomon succeeds him.

l: Solomon, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 29
s: Solomon is described by David as the son whom God alone has chosen, yet young and tender, and he is the one to build the house. He is made king a second time and anointed before the LORD, then sits on the LORD's throne and prospers. All Israel, the princes, the mighty men, and David's other sons submit to him, and the LORD magnifies him with royal majesty greater than any previous king of Israel.

l: LORD, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 29
s: The LORD is praised by David as the owner of greatness, power, glory, victory, majesty, and the kingdom, and the source of riches and honor. David says the people give only what already comes from his hand and that he tests hearts and delights in uprightness. The LORD is blessed by the assembly, receives their sacrifices, and magnifies Solomon in the sight of all Israel.

l: God's house, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 29
s: David says the house is not for man but for the LORD God, and he has prepared materials of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and precious stones for it. Gold and silver are designated to overlay the walls and for the work of artisans. David prays that Solomon will be given a perfect heart to build it.

l: children of Israel, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 29
s: The assembly hears David's appeal and rejoices as the people give willingly. At David's call they bless the LORD, bow down and prostrate themselves before the LORD and the king, and offer sacrifices. They eat and drink with great gladness, make Solomon king a second time, and anoint him, with Zadok as priest.

l: leaders who offered willingly, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 29
s: The princes of the fathers' households, the princes of the tribes, the captains of thousands and hundreds, and the rulers over the king's work respond to David's call by offering willingly. Their gifts are five thousand talents and ten thousand darics of gold, ten thousand talents of silver, eighteen thousand talents of bronze, and one hundred thousand talents of iron. Their willing, wholehearted giving causes the people and David to rejoice.

l: offerings for the temple, 1 Chronicles, Chapter 29
s: David gives three thousand talents of gold of Ophir and seven thousand talents of refined silver from his own treasure, besides his earlier preparations. The leaders add gold, silver, bronze, and iron, and others give precious stones, which are placed in the treasury under Jehiel the Gershonite. David acknowledges that all of it comes from the LORD and was merely given back to him.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles / Chapter 1
s: Solomon son of David is established in his kingdom, with the LORD his God making him exceedingly great. He gathers Israel's leaders and the assembly and goes to the high place at Gibeon, where the Tent of Meeting and the bronze altar made by Bezalel stand, and offers one thousand burnt offerings. That night God appears and invites him to ask, and Solomon requests wisdom and knowledge to judge the people, so God grants these and promises riches, wealth, and honor unmatched by any other king. Solomon returns to Jerusalem and reigns over Israel, gathering 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, making silver and gold as common as stones, and trading horses and chariots from Egypt and Kue to the Hittite and Syrian kings.

l: Solomon, The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles / Chapter 1
s: Solomon son of David is firmly established in his kingdom, offers one thousand burnt offerings at Gibeon, and asks God for wisdom and knowledge to judge the people. God grants this and promises him unmatched riches, wealth, and honor; he then reigns from Jerusalem, amassing chariots and horsemen and trading horses and chariots.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles / Chapter 1
s: The LORD, Solomon's God, is with Solomon and makes him exceedingly great. As God, he appears to Solomon at night, praises him for not asking for riches or long life, and grants wisdom and knowledge along with riches, wealth, and honor beyond any other king.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles / Chapter 1
s: Solomon speaks to all Israel, including captains, judges, princes, and heads of the fathers' households, and reigns over Israel after returning from Gibeon. Solomon describes Israel as a great people, like the dust of the earth in multitude.

l: Gibeon, The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles / Chapter 1
s: Gibeon is the site of the high place where Solomon and the assembly go, because God's Tent of Meeting is there. Solomon offers a thousand burnt offerings there, and God appears to him that night; he then leaves Gibeon for Jerusalem.

l: Tent of Meeting, The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles / Chapter 1
s: The Tent of Meeting, which the LORD's servant Moses made in the wilderness, is at the high place at Gibeon. Solomon and the assembly go there, and the bronze altar stands before it.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles / Chapter 1
s: Jerusalem is where David pitched a tent for God's ark after bringing it up from Kiriath Jearim. Solomon returns there from Gibeon, keeps chariots and horsemen there with him, and makes silver, gold, and cedars as common as stones and sycamores there.

l: bronze altar, The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles / Chapter 1
s: The bronze altar was made by Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, and stands before the LORD's tabernacle at Gibeon. Solomon goes up to it and offers one thousand burnt offerings on it.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 2
s: Solomon resolves to build a house for the LORD's name and a house for his kingdom, and assigns seventy thousand burden bearers, eighty thousand stone cutters, and three thousand six hundred overseers. He sends a message to Huram, king of Tyre, asking for a skilled craftsman and for cedar, cypress, and algum timber from Lebanon, and he offers wheat, barley, wine, and oil in payment. Solomon explains that the house will be great because his God is greater than all gods, though heaven cannot contain him. Huram answers in writing, blesses the LORD, sends the skilled man Huram-abi, agrees to cut the wood and float it by sea to Joppa, and asks that the provisions be sent. Solomon then counts the foreigners in Israel, finding 153,600, and sets them to the same labor of bearing burdens, cutting stone, and overseeing.

l: Solomon, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 2
s: Solomon decides to build a house for the LORD's name and a house for his kingdom, and counts out 70,000 burden bearers, 80,000 stone cutters, and 3,600 overseers. He asks Huram of Tyre for a skilled craftsman and Lebanon timber, promising wheat, barley, wine, and oil, and says no one can truly build God a house, so the purpose is to burn incense before him. He also counts the foreigners in Israel, finding 153,600, and assigns them to labor.

l: Huram, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 2
s: Huram, king of Tyre, replies in writing to Solomon, saying the LORD loves his people and made Solomon king over them, and he blesses the LORD, the God of Israel. He sends the skilled man Huram-abi, agrees to cut wood in Lebanon and bring it by sea in rafts to Joppa, and asks that the promised wheat, barley, oil, and wine be sent to his servants.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 2
s: The LORD is described by Solomon as the God of Israel, greater than all gods, whom heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain. Huram blesses him as the maker of heaven and earth who gave David a wise son, and says he loves his people and made Solomon king over them.

l: Huram-abi, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 2
s: Huram-abi is sent by Huram to Solomon as a skillful man endowed with understanding. He is the son of a woman of the daughters of Dan and a father from Tyre, and he is skilled in working gold, silver, bronze, iron, stone, timber, purple, blue, fine linen, and crimson, and in engraving and devising any device. He is to be placed with Solomon's skillful men and those of David.

l: LORD's temple, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 2
s: Solomon plans it as a house for the name of the LORD, for dedication to him, for burning incense, the continual show bread, and burnt offerings on Sabbaths, new moons, and set feasts. He says it will be great and wonderful because God is greater than all gods, and he arranges workers, craftsmen, timber, and provisions for it.

l: burden bearers (Solomon's), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 2
s: Solomon counts out seventy thousand men to bear burdens for the building work. The same number of the foreigners in Israel are later set to bear burdens as well.

l: stone cutters (Solomon's), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 2
s: Solomon counts out eighty thousand men as stone cutters in the mountains, with overseers set over them. Eighty thousand of the foreigners are later also set as stone cutters in the mountains.

l: foreigners in Israel, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 2
s: Solomon counts the foreigners in the land of Israel, following the census David had taken, and finds 153,600. He sets seventy thousand of them to bear burdens, eighty thousand to cut stone in the mountains, and 3,600 to be overseers assigning the people their work.

l: timber (cedar, cypress, algum), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 2
s: Solomon asks Huram for cedar, cypress, and algum trees from Lebanon, noting that Huram's servants know how to cut timber there, and offers wheat, barley, wine, and oil to the cutters. Huram agrees to cut as much wood as needed and bring it in rafts by sea to Joppa, from where Solomon's people will carry it up to Jerusalem.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 3
s: Chapter 3 describes Solomon beginning to build the LORD's house at Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, in the second month of the fourth year of his reign. It gives the foundation dimensions of sixty by twenty cubits and details the porch, the larger room, and the lavish gold overlay and decoration with precious stones, palm trees, chains, and cherubim. It describes the most holy place, where two carved cherubim with wings spanning twenty cubits stood facing the house, and a veil of blue, purple, crimson, and fine linen. Finally, Solomon sets up two thirty-five-cubit pillars before the temple, topped with chains and one hundred pomegranates, and names them Jachin on the right and Boaz on the left.

l: Solomon, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 3
s: Solomon began building the LORD's house at Jerusalem on Mount Moriah in the second month of the fourth year of his reign. He laid the foundations, overlaid the house with gold, made the most holy place, the cherubim, the veil, and the two pillars, and named the pillars Jachin and Boaz.

l: LORD's temple, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 3
s: The LORD's house was built on Mount Moriah at the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, where the LORD appeared to David. Its foundation measured sixty cubits by twenty cubits, with a porch twenty cubits wide at the front, and its beams, thresholds, walls, and doors were overlaid with gold and engraved with cherubim. Its larger room had a cypress ceiling overlaid with fine gold and ornamented with palm trees and chains, and the house was decorated with precious stones and gold from Parvaim.

l: temple (the LORD's house), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 3
s: Solomon made the most holy place twenty cubits long and twenty cubits wide, overlaying it with fine gold amounting to six hundred talents. The nails weighed fifty shekels of gold, and two carved cherubim were placed within it.

l: cherubim (in the most holy place), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 3
s: Two cherubim were made by carving in the most holy place and overlaid with gold. Each had wings of five cubits each, one reaching the wall and the other touching the other cherub's wing, so together they spread twenty cubits. They stood on their feet with their faces toward the house.

l: Jachin, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 3
s: Jachin is the name Solomon gave to the pillar set up on the right hand before the temple.

l: Boaz, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 3
s: Boaz is the name Solomon gave to the pillar set up on the left hand before the temple.

l: pillars (before the temple), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 3
s: Solomon made two pillars before the house, thirty-five cubits high, each with a capital of five cubits on top. Chains were made and put on the tops of the pillars along with one hundred pomegranates. He set them up one on the right and one on the left, naming them Jachin and Boaz.

l: building of the temple, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 3
s: The building began on the second day of the second month in the fourth year of Solomon's reign, on the site David had prepared and appointed. The foundations were laid by the first measure of sixty by twenty cubits, and the work included extensive gold overlay, precious stones, carved cherubim, a veil, and two front pillars.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 4
s: Chapter 4 describes the furnishings Solomon had made for God's house. These include a bronze altar, a great molten sea resting on twelve oxen, ten basins, ten gold lamp stands, ten tables, and a hundred gold basins, along with the court of the priests and its bronze-overlaid doors. Huram (also called Huram-abi) made the pots, shovels, forks, basins, pillars, capitals, networks, and pomegranates for King Solomon. The king cast the bronze vessels in the clay ground of the Jordan plain between Succoth and Zeredah, in such abundance that the bronze could not be weighed. The chapter ends by listing the golden altar, tables, lamp stands, and utensils of pure gold, and the gold doors of the temple.

l: Solomon, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 4
s: Solomon is the king for whom all the bronze and gold furnishings of God's house were made, and he is said to have made the altar, basins, lamp stands, tables, court, and vessels. He cast the bronze vessels in the clay ground of the Jordan plain between Succoth and Zeredah, producing so many that the weight of the bronze could not be determined.

l: Huram, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 4
s: Huram, also called Huram-abi, made the pots, shovels, forks, and basins, and finished the work he did for King Solomon in God's house. This included the two pillars, their bowls and capitals, the two networks, the four hundred pomegranates, the bases with their basins, and the sea with its twelve oxen.

l: molten sea, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 4
s: The molten sea was ten cubits from brim to brim, five cubits high, and thirty cubits in circumference, with a thickness of a handbreadth and a brim like a cup or lily flower. It stood on twelve oxen facing the four directions, three each, with their hindquarters inward, held three thousand baths, and was for the priests to wash in. It was set on the right side of the house, eastward toward the south.

l: LORD's temple, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 4
s: God's house received the furnishings Solomon made, including the ten gold lamp stands and ten tables set five on each side in the temple, the sea, basins, and the golden altar. Its court of the priests and great court had bronze-overlaid doors, and the inner doors to the most holy place and the doors of the main hall were of gold.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 5
s: Solomon finishes all the work on the LORD's house and places the things his father David had dedicated, the silver, gold, and vessels, in the treasuries of God's house. He assembles the elders, tribal heads, and fathers' household princes of Israel at Jerusalem in the seventh month to bring the ark of the LORD's covenant up from David's city, Zion. The Levites and Levitical priests carry up the ark, the Tent of Meeting, and the holy vessels, while Solomon and the congregation sacrifice innumerable sheep and cattle. The priests set the ark in the most holy place under the cherubim's wings; it contains only the two tablets Moses put there at Horeb. When the priests come out and the Levite singers and trumpeters praise the LORD as one voice, a cloud fills the house so that the priests cannot stand to minister, for the LORD's glory fills God's house.

l: Solomon, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 5
s: Solomon finished all the work on the LORD's house and put the silver, gold, and vessels dedicated by his father David into the treasuries of God's house. He assembled Israel's elders and leaders at Jerusalem to bring up the ark, and he and the congregation sacrificed sheep and cattle too numerous to count before it.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 5
s: The LORD had made a covenant with the children of Israel at Horeb when they came out of Egypt. He was praised as good, with loving kindness enduring forever, and his glory filled God's house in a cloud so that the priests could not stand to minister.

l: ark of the LORD's covenant, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 5
s: The ark was brought up from David's city, Zion, by the Levites and Levitical priests, together with the Tent of Meeting and its holy vessels. The priests placed it in the inner sanctuary, the most holy place, under the cherubim's wings; its poles' ends were visible from the front of the inner sanctuary but not outside, and it contained only the two tablets Moses put there at Horeb.

l: LORD's temple, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 5
s: The house was completed, and its treasuries received the dedicated silver, gold, and vessels. The ark was installed in its inner sanctuary, and at the end of the ceremony a cloud filled the house because the LORD's glory filled it.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 5
s: The elders of Israel, the tribal heads, and the princes of the fathers' households assembled at Jerusalem, and all the men of Israel gathered to the king at the feast in the seventh month. The congregation sacrificed countless sheep and cattle before the ark.

l: Levites, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 5
s: The Levites took up the ark, and the Levitical priests brought up the ark, the Tent of Meeting, and the holy vessels. The Levites who were singers also stood at the east end of the altar to praise the LORD.

l: priests, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 5
s: The priests brought the ark into the most holy place under the cherubim's wings. All the priests present had sanctified themselves and did not keep their divisions; one hundred twenty of them sounded trumpets, and they were unable to stand and minister because of the cloud.

l: Levite singers, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 5
s: The Levite singers, including Asaph, Heman, Jeduthun, and their sons and brothers, stood at the east end of the altar in fine linen with cymbals, stringed instruments, and harps. Together with the trumpeters they made one sound in praising and thanking the LORD.

l: cloud (filling the LORD's house), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 5
s: A cloud filled the LORD's house as the singers and trumpeters praised him. It prevented the priests from standing to minister, because it signified that the LORD's glory filled God's house.

l: praise of the LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 5
s: The trumpeters and singers were as one, lifting their voices with trumpets, cymbals, and instruments to praise and thank the LORD, saying he is good and his loving kindness endures forever. The house was then filled with a cloud.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 6
s: Solomon addresses the assembly of Israel, blessing the LORD for fulfilling his word to David by letting Solomon, David's son, build the house for the LORD's name. Standing on a bronze platform with hands spread toward heaven, he prays that the LORD keep his promise of a throne to David's line if his children walk in the LORD's law. He acknowledges that heaven cannot contain God, much less the house, yet asks God to hear prayers made toward it. He then lists situations in which people may pray toward the house, including oaths, defeat, drought, famine, foreigners, battle and captivity, asking the LORD to hear from heaven and forgive. He closes by asking the LORD to arise into his resting place and to remember his loving kindnesses to David.

l: Solomon, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 6
s: Solomon blesses the assembly of Israel and the LORD, declaring that he has built the house and sits on his father David's throne as promised. He kneels on a bronze platform in the court, spreads his hands toward heaven, and prays at length, asking the LORD to hear prayers made toward the house and to remember David.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 6
s: The LORD is said to have dwelt in thick darkness, to have chosen Jerusalem and David, and to have fulfilled with his hand what he spoke to David. Solomon describes him as a God who keeps covenant and loving kindness, whom heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain, and who alone knows the hearts of men. He is asked to hear from heaven, forgive, judge, and maintain the cause of those who pray toward the house.

l: David, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 6
s: David is recalled as having had it in his heart to build a house for the LORD's name, and the LORD said he did well but that his son would build it instead. He was chosen to be over Israel and received the LORD's promise of a throne. Solomon asks the LORD to remember his loving kindnesses to David.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 6
s: The assembly of Israel stands while Solomon blesses them and prays before them. Solomon asks the LORD to hear and forgive Israel when they pray toward the house, whether after defeat, drought, famine, plague, battle or captivity. He also asks that the LORD bring them back to their land when they repent, and that they fear him and walk in his ways.

l: LORD's temple, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 6
s: The house is built by Solomon for the name of the LORD, and the ark holding the LORD's covenant is set there. Solomon admits that even heaven cannot contain God, much less this house, yet asks that God's eyes be open toward it day and night. It becomes the place toward which Israelites and foreigners are to direct their prayers, so that all peoples may know it is called by God's name.

l: covenant with David, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 6
s: Solomon says the LORD has fulfilled his promise to David by putting Solomon on the throne of Israel and letting him build the house. He asks the LORD to keep the further promise that David will never lack a man to sit on the throne, on the condition that his children take heed to walk in the LORD's law. He asks that the LORD's word to David be verified.

l: Solomon's prayer of dedication, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 6
s: The prayer begins by praising the LORD as incomparable and as keeper of covenant, then asks that he hear prayers made toward the house. It lists cases such as oaths, defeat, drought, famine, plague, the foreigner, battle and exile, each asking the LORD to hear from heaven, forgive and act. It ends with a plea for the LORD to arise into his resting place and not turn away the face of his anointed.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 7
s: When Solomon finishes praying, fire comes down from heaven and consumes the offerings, and the LORD's glory fills the house so that the priests cannot enter. Solomon and all the people offer huge sacrifices, dedicate the house, and hold a seven-day dedication of the altar followed by a seven-day feast, with Levites and priests making music and giving thanks. On the twenty-third day of the seventh month Solomon sends the people home joyful. The LORD then appears to Solomon by night, saying he has chosen the house, promising to hear and heal if his people humble themselves and pray, and promising to establish Solomon's throne if he walks as David did. He also warns that if they forsake him and serve other gods, he will uproot them from the land and cast the house out of his sight, making it a byword.

l: Solomon, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 7
s: Solomon finishes praying, offers twenty-two thousand cattle and a hundred twenty thousand sheep, and makes the middle of the court holy because the bronze altar cannot hold the offerings. He holds the feast for seven days, sends the people home, and completes the LORD's house and his own. The LORD appears to him by night, promising to establish his throne if he walks as David did and warning of consequences if he turns away.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 7
s: The LORD sends fire from heaven, fills the house with his glory, and appears to Solomon by night saying he has heard his prayer and chosen the place. He promises to hear, forgive, and heal the land if his people humble themselves, pray, seek his face, and turn from wicked ways. He also covenants to establish Solomon's throne if Solomon obeys, and warns of uprooting the people and rejecting the house if they serve other gods.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 7
s: All the children of Israel watch the fire come down, bow with their faces to the ground, worship, and give thanks that the LORD is good and his loving kindness endures forever. They offer sacrifices, keep the feast from the entrance of Hamath to the brook of Egypt, and are sent home joyful on the twenty-third day of the seventh month. The LORD warns that if they forsake him, he will pluck them up from the land he gave them.

l: LORD's temple, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 7
s: The LORD's glory fills the house so that the priests cannot enter it, and it is dedicated by the king and all the people. The LORD says he has chosen and made it holy so his name, eyes, and heart will be there forever, and that prayer made there will be heard. He warns that if the people turn away, he will cast it out of his sight and make it a proverb and byword, astonishing all who pass by.

l: fire from heaven, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 7
s: Fire comes down from heaven after Solomon finishes praying and consumes the burnt offering and the sacrifices. The people watching it bow to the ground, worship, and give thanks to the LORD.

l: sacrifices and offerings, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 7
s: The fire consumes the burnt offering and sacrifices, and the king and all the people offer sacrifices before the LORD, including Solomon's twenty-two thousand cattle and a hundred twenty thousand sheep. Because the bronze altar cannot receive the burnt offering, meal offering, and fat, Solomon makes the middle of the court holy to offer them there.

l: dedication feast, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 7
s: Solomon and all Israel keep the dedication of the altar for seven days and the feast for seven days, with a solemn assembly on the eighth day. Priests sound trumpets and Levites play instruments David made to give thanks. On the twenty-third day of the seventh month the people are sent home joyful and glad of heart.

l: warning of judgment, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 7
s: The LORD warns that if Solomon and the people turn away, forsake his statutes, and serve other gods, he will pluck them up by the roots from their land and cast the house out of his sight. The house will become a proverb and byword, and passersby will ask why, and be told the people abandoned the LORD who brought them out of Egypt and so received this evil.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 8
s: After twenty years of building the LORD's house and his own house, Solomon rebuilt the cities Huram had given him, settled Israelites in them, and prevailed against Hamath Zobah. He built Tadmor, Beth Horon the upper and lower, Baalath, storage cities, and cities for chariots and horsemen, and conscripted forced labor from the Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, while making no servants of Israelites, who served as warriors and officers. He moved Pharaoh's daughter out of David's city to a house he built for her, because places where the LORD's ark had come were holy. Solomon offered burnt offerings on the LORD's altar according to Moses' commandment and set the priests and Levites in their divisions according to David's ordinance, and the LORD's house was completed. He then went to Ezion Geber and Eloth, where Huram sent ships and servants, and they brought four hundred fifty talents of gold from Ophir to him.

l: Solomon, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 8
s: Solomon, at the end of twenty years of building the LORD's house and his own, rebuilt cities, prevailed against Hamath Zobah, and conscripted forced labor from the remaining peoples but not from Israelites. He moved Pharaoh's daughter to her own house, offered burnt offerings as Moses commanded, organized the priests and Levites per David's ordinance, and received four hundred fifty talents of gold from Ophir via ships Huram sent.

l: LORD's temple, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 8
s: The LORD's house was completed, with all Solomon's work accomplished from the day of its foundation until it was finished. Its altar stood before the porch, and the places where the LORD's ark had come were called holy.

l: cities built by Solomon, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 8
s: Solomon built the cities Huram had given him and settled Israelites there, and built Tadmor, storage cities in Hamath, Beth Horon the upper and lower (fortified with walls, gates, and bars), and Baalath. He also built cities for his chariots and horsemen and whatever he desired in Jerusalem, Lebanon, and all his dominion.

l: remaining peoples conscripted for forced labor, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 8
s: The Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites who were left in the land and not consumed by Israel were conscripted by Solomon for forced labor, which continued to the day of writing. Unlike them, the Israelites were not made servants but served as men of war and officers.

l: burnt offerings, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 8
s: Solomon offered burnt offerings to the LORD on the LORD's altar before the porch, as each day's duty required. He offered them according to Moses' commandment on the Sabbaths, new moons, and the three yearly feasts of unleavened bread, weeks, and booths.

l: priests, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 8
s: Solomon appointed the divisions of the priests to their service according to the ordinance of David, who was called the man of God. The priests and Levites did not depart from the king's commandment concerning any matter or the treasures.

l: Levites, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 8
s: Solomon appointed the Levites to their offices according to David's ordinance, to praise and minister before the priests as each day required. The doorkeepers served by divisions at every gate, and the Levites did not depart from the king's commandment concerning any matter or the treasures.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 9
s: The queen of Sheba comes to Jerusalem with a great caravan to test King Solomon with hard questions, and she is overwhelmed by his wisdom, house, and court. She blesses the LORD, gives Solomon gold, spices, and precious stones, and receives all she desired before returning to her land. The chapter then describes Solomon's vast wealth: 666 talents of gold in a year, gold shields, an ivory and gold throne with lions, gold vessels, and ships of Tarshish bringing treasure with Huram's servants. Kings of the earth seek him out and bring tribute, and he rules from the River to the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt. The chapter closes by citing the prophetic records of his acts, noting he reigned forty years, was buried in David's city, and was succeeded by his son Rehoboam.

l: Solomon, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 9
s: Solomon answered all the questions of the queen of Sheba, received her gifts, and gave her all she desired. He made gold shields, an ivory throne overlaid with gold, and gold vessels, was visited and paid tribute by kings, and ruled from the River to the land of the Philistines and the border of Egypt. He reigned in Jerusalem forty years, slept with his fathers, was buried in David's city, and was succeeded by his son Rehoboam.

l: queen of Sheba, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 9
s: The queen of Sheba came to Jerusalem with a very great caravan to test Solomon with hard questions, and was left with no more spirit in her upon seeing his wisdom and court. She affirmed the report she had heard was true, blessed the LORD, gave Solomon 120 talents of gold, spices, and precious stones, and then returned to her own land with her servants after Solomon gave her all she asked.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 9
s: The LORD is blessed by the queen of Sheba as the God who delighted in Solomon, set him on the throne, and loved Israel to establish them forever. Solomon's house for the LORD has terraces of algum wood and an ascent by which the king goes up to it. God is said to have put wisdom in Solomon's heart.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 9
s: Jerusalem is where the queen of Sheba came to test Solomon, and where the LORD's house and the king's house stand. Solomon stationed horsemen there, made silver as common as stones in it, reigned there over all Israel forty years, and his son Rehoboam took over his reign after him.

l: Solomon’s wisdom, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 9
s: Solomon's wisdom let him answer all the queen of Sheba's questions, and she said half of its greatness had not been told her and that he exceeded its fame. All the kings of the earth sought his presence to hear the wisdom God had put in his heart, and he exceeded them all in wisdom and riches.

l: Solomon’s riches, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 9
s: Solomon received 666 talents of gold in one year, besides what traders, merchants, Arabian kings, and governors brought, and he made gold shields, a great ivory and gold throne, and gold drinking vessels, so that silver was not considered valuable. Ships of Tarshish brought gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks every three years, kings brought yearly tribute, and he held four thousand stalls and twelve thousand horsemen.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 10
s: All Israel gathers at Shechem to make Rehoboam king, and Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who had fled to Egypt from Solomon, returns at their call. Jeroboam and the people ask Rehoboam to lighten the heavy yoke Solomon put on them in exchange for their service. Rehoboam consults the old men who served Solomon, who advise kindness, but he abandons their counsel and follows the young men who grew up with him, who urge him to add to the yoke. He answers the people roughly, and the text says this was brought about by God to establish his word spoken by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam. Israel renounces any portion in David and departs to their tents, only the people in Judah's cities remain under Rehoboam, and when Rehoboam sends Hadoram over forced labor, Israel stones him to death and Rehoboam flees to Jerusalem.

l: Rehoboam, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 10
s: Rehoboam goes to Shechem to be made king, asks the people for three days, and consults first the old men and then the young men. He abandons the old men's counsel and answers the people roughly, promising to add to the yoke and chastise with scorpions. He reigns only over the Israelites in Judah's cities, and after Hadoram is stoned he hurries to his chariot to flee to Jerusalem.

l: Jeroboam, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 10
s: Jeroboam, who had fled to Egypt from King Solomon, returns when Israel sends for him. He and all Israel speak to Rehoboam asking for a lighter yoke and come back on the third day. The text notes that God's word spoken to him by Ahijah the Shilonite was being established through these events.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 10
s: All Israel gathers at Shechem to make Rehoboam king and petitions him to lighten the yoke in return for service. When the king refuses to listen, they declare they have no portion in David and depart to their tents. They stone Hadoram to death and rebel against David's house.

l: Solomon, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 10
s: Solomon is described as the father of Rehoboam who made the people's yoke grievous and heavy and chastised them with whips. Jeroboam had fled from his presence to Egypt, and the old men had stood before him while he lived.

l: old men (Solomon's counselors), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 10
s: The old men, who had stood before Solomon while he lived, are consulted by Rehoboam. They advise him to be kind, please the people and speak good words, so that the people will be his servants forever. Rehoboam abandons their counsel.

l: young men (Rehoboam's peers), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 10
s: The young men who grew up with Rehoboam and stood before him advise him to say that his little finger is thicker than his father's waist. They urge him to add to the yoke and chastise with scorpions rather than whips. Rehoboam follows their counsel.

l: David's house, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 10
s: Israel renounces any portion or inheritance in David and the son of Jesse, telling David to see to his own house. Israel rebels against David's house, a state the text says continues to this day. Only the Israelites living in Judah's cities remain under Rehoboam.

l: heavy yoke (Solomon's burdens on Israel), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 10
s: The people describe the yoke and grievous service Solomon put on them and ask for it to be made lighter. Rehoboam instead promises to add to it, and sends Hadoram, who was over the men subject to forced labor. The yoke thus becomes the cause of Israel's break from Rehoboam.

l: Israel's rebellion (division of the kingdom), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 10
s: After Rehoboam refuses to listen, Israel departs to their tents and only those in Judah's cities stay under him. The text says the outcome was brought about by God to establish his word through Ahijah. Israel's stoning of Hadoram and Rehoboam's flight to Jerusalem seal the break, which the text says lasts to this day.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 11
s: Rehoboam gathers 180,000 chosen warriors from Judah and Benjamin to fight Israel, but the LORD sends Shemaiah the man of God to forbid it, and the men return home. Rehoboam lives in Jerusalem and fortifies fifteen cities in Judah and Benjamin with captains, food stores, shields and spears. Priests, Levites and faithful Israelites leave Jeroboam, who had cast the Levites off and appointed his own priests for the high places and calf idols, and come to Judah and Jerusalem, strengthening Rehoboam for three years. Rehoboam takes eighteen wives and sixty concubines, loves Maacah most, and appoints her son Abijah as chief prince intending to make him king. He also disperses some of his sons to the fortified cities and provides them with food and wives.

l: Rehoboam, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 11
s: Rehoboam assembles 180,000 warriors to fight Israel but turns back when the LORD forbids it through Shemaiah. He fortifies cities in Judah, is strengthened for three years by those who come to him, and fathers twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters by eighteen wives and sixty concubines. He loves Maacah above all and appoints her son Abijah chief prince, intending him to be king.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 11
s: Rehoboam comes to Jerusalem and lives there. The Levites and those from all the tribes of Israel who set their hearts to seek the LORD come to Jerusalem to sacrifice to the LORD.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 11
s: Judah, with Benjamin, belongs to Rehoboam, who builds and fortifies cities there. It is strengthened by the Levites, priests and faithful Israelites who come to it, and Rehoboam disperses his sons throughout its lands.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 11
s: Israel is the kingdom Rehoboam intends to fight and bring back under his rule, but the LORD forbids the attack, calling Israel the brothers of Judah. Priests, Levites and those from its tribes who seek the LORD leave to go to Judah and Jerusalem.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 11
s: The LORD sends His word to Shemaiah the man of God, forbidding Rehoboam and Judah from fighting their brothers and saying the matter is of Him. The people obey. He is the God of Israel's fathers, sought by those who come to Jerusalem to sacrifice.

l: Jeroboam, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 11
s: Jeroboam is the one against whom Rehoboam's men turn back from going. He and his sons cast off the Levites from the priest's office to the LORD, and he appoints his own priests for the high places and for the male goat and calf idols he made.

l: fortified cities (Rehoboam's), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 11
s: Rehoboam builds and fortifies fifteen cities in Judah and Benjamin, including Bethlehem, Tekoa, Lachish and Hebron. He places captains in them with stores of food, oil and wine, and puts shields and spears in each. Later he disperses some of his sons to every fortified city with abundant food.

l: priests and Levites, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 11
s: The priests and Levites from all Israel leave their pasture lands and possessions and stand with Rehoboam in Judah and Jerusalem, because Jeroboam and his sons cast them off from serving the LORD as priests. Jeroboam instead appoints his own priests for the high places.

l: Maacah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 11
s: Maacah, granddaughter of Absalom, becomes Rehoboam's wife after Mahalath and bears Abijah, Attai, Ziza and Shelomith. Rehoboam loves her above all his other wives and concubines.

l: Abijah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 11
s: Abijah is a son of Rehoboam and Maacah. Rehoboam appoints him chief, the prince among his brothers, because he intends to make him king.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 12
s: Once Rehoboam's kingdom was established and strong, he and all Israel abandoned the LORD's law. In Rehoboam's fifth year, Shishak king of Egypt invaded with a vast army, took Judah's fortified cities, and came to Jerusalem. The prophet Shemaiah told Rehoboam and the princes that the LORD had left them in Shishak's hand, and they humbled themselves, so the LORD granted some deliverance but made them Shishak's servants. Shishak took the treasures of the LORD's house and the king's house, including Solomon's gold shields, which Rehoboam replaced with bronze ones. Rehoboam reigned seventeen years, did evil by not seeking the LORD, fought continually with Jeroboam, and was succeeded by his son Abijah.

l: Rehoboam, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 12
s: Rehoboam, once strong, abandoned the LORD's law along with all Israel, and then humbled himself when Shemaiah delivered the LORD's message. After Shishak took the gold shields, he made bronze ones and had the guards carry them whenever he entered the LORD's house. He began to reign at forty-one, reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, did evil by not setting his heart to seek the LORD, and was buried in David's city, succeeded by his son Abijah.

l: Shishak, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 12
s: Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem in Rehoboam's fifth year with twelve hundred chariots, sixty thousand horsemen, and countless Lubim, Sukkiim, and Ethiopians. He took Judah's fortified cities, then took all the treasures of the LORD's house and the king's house, along with Solomon's gold shields. The LORD said Judah would become his servants, though his wrath would not be poured out on Jerusalem by Shishak's hand.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 12
s: The LORD left Rehoboam and the princes in Shishak's hand because they had forsaken him. When they humbled themselves, he spoke to Shemaiah, promising not to destroy them but to grant some deliverance, while still making them servants so they would know his service. His wrath turned from Rehoboam, and Jerusalem is identified as the city he chose out of all the tribes of Israel to put his name there.

l: Shemaiah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 12
s: Shemaiah the prophet came to Rehoboam and the princes of Judah gathered at Jerusalem and told them the LORD had left them in Shishak's hand because they forsook him. He later received the LORD's word that they would be spared destruction. His histories are named as a record of Rehoboam's acts, along with those of Iddo the seer.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 12
s: Jerusalem was the target of Shishak's attack, where Judah's princes gathered and the king and princes humbled themselves. Its wrath-bringing devastation was averted, though Shishak took the treasures of the LORD's house and the king's house. It is described as the city the LORD chose out of all Israel's tribes to put his name there, where Rehoboam reigned seventeen years.

l: Shishak's invasion of Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 12
s: In Rehoboam's fifth year, Shishak came with a huge army, took Judah's fortified cities, and reached Jerusalem, because the people had trespassed against the LORD. After the leaders humbled themselves, the LORD limited the outcome: Jerusalem was not destroyed, but Shishak carried off the temple and royal treasures and Solomon's gold shields, and Judah became his servants.

l: Rehoboam's humbling, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 12
s: After Shemaiah's message, Rehoboam and the princes humbled themselves and said, "The LORD is righteous." Seeing this, the LORD promised some deliverance and no destruction, and his wrath turned from Rehoboam so that he was not destroyed altogether. The text also notes that good things were found in Judah.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 13
s: In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam, Abijah began to reign over Judah for three years; his mother was Micaiah the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. War broke out between Abijah, with 400,000 chosen men, and Jeroboam, with 800,000. From Mount Zemaraim, Abijah told Jeroboam and Israel that the LORD gave the kingdom to David's line, that Israel had adopted golden calves and false priests, and that Judah still kept the LORD's worship. Jeroboam ambushed Judah from behind, but Judah cried to the LORD, the priests sounded trumpets, and God struck Jeroboam and Israel, so that 500,000 Israelites fell. Abijah took Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron with their villages, Jeroboam never recovered and was struck by the LORD and died, and Abijah grew mighty with fourteen wives and thirty-eight children.

l: Abijah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 13
s: Abijah began to reign over Judah in the eighteenth year of Jeroboam and reigned three years in Jerusalem; his mother was Micaiah daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. He addressed Jeroboam and Israel from Mount Zemaraim, then led Judah to victory, pursued Jeroboam, and took Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron with their villages. He grew mighty, took fourteen wives, and fathered twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters; his other acts are written in the commentary of the prophet Iddo.

l: Jeroboam, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 13
s: Jeroboam, son of Nebat and former servant of Solomon, is described by Abijah as having rebelled against his lord and made golden calves for Israel. He set 800,000 chosen men against Abijah and sent an ambush behind Judah, but God struck him and Israel, and he lost 500,000 men and several cities. He never recovered strength in Abijah's days, and the LORD struck him and he died.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 13
s: Judah, under Abijah, fought Israel with 400,000 chosen men and was caught between Jeroboam's army and an ambush. They cried to the LORD, the priests sounded trumpets, and the men of Judah shouted, and they prevailed because they relied on the LORD, the God of their fathers.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 13
s: Israel, led by Jeroboam, was accused by Abijah of keeping golden calves and driving out the LORD's priests and Levites. The children of Israel fled before Judah, 500,000 chosen men fell slain, and they were brought under at that time.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 13
s: The LORD, the God of Israel, is said by Abijah to have given the kingdom over Israel to David and his sons by a covenant of salt, and to be served by Judah's priests and Levites. God struck Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah and delivered them into Judah's hand, and later the LORD struck Jeroboam so that he died.

l: battle between Abijah and Jeroboam, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 13
s: The battle pitted Abijah's 400,000 chosen men against Jeroboam's 800,000, with Jeroboam's ambush placing Judah between two fronts. After Judah cried to the LORD, the priests sounded trumpets, and Judah shouted, God struck Israel, and 500,000 Israelites fell in a great slaughter. Judah prevailed because they relied on the LORD, and Abijah then took Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 14
s: Abijah dies and is buried in David's city, and his son Asa becomes king, enjoying ten years of quiet in the land. Asa does what is good in the LORD's eyes by removing foreign altars, high places, pillars, Asherah poles and sun images, and by commanding Judah to seek the LORD. Because the LORD gives rest, Asa has Judah build fortified cities with walls, towers, gates and bars, and he musters 300,000 men from Judah and 280,000 from Benjamin. Zerah the Ethiopian comes against them at Mareshah with a million troops and three hundred chariots, and Asa cries to the LORD for help. The LORD strikes the Ethiopians, who flee, and Asa and his people pursue them to Gerar, plunder the surrounding cities and the livestock tents, and return to Jerusalem.

l: Asa, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 14
s: Asa succeeds his father Abijah as king and does what is good and right in the LORD's eyes, removing foreign altars, high places, pillars, Asherah poles and sun images. He builds fortified cities during ten quiet years, fields an army of 580,000 men, and when Zerah attacks he cries to the LORD for help. He pursues the fleeing Ethiopians to Gerar, plunders the area, and returns to Jerusalem.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 14
s: The LORD is sought by Judah at Asa's command and gives the land rest on every side. When Asa cries to him, he strikes the Ethiopians before Asa and Judah, causing them to flee and be destroyed. His fear falls on the cities around Gerar.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 14
s: Judah is commanded by Asa to seek the LORD and obey his law, and it builds fortified cities with walls, towers, gates and bars, prospering in the quiet. Its army of 300,000 bearing bucklers and spears fights with Asa, defeats the Ethiopians, and returns to Jerusalem with abundant booty, sheep and camels.

l: Zerah the Ethiopian, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 14
s: Zerah comes out against Asa with an army of a million troops and three hundred chariots, reaching Mareshah. His forces are struck by the LORD and flee before Asa and Judah.

l: Ethiopians, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 14
s: The Ethiopians, Zerah's army, are struck by the LORD before Asa and Judah and flee. So many fall during the pursuit to Gerar that they cannot recover, and they are destroyed before the LORD and his army.

l: Battle between Asa and Zerah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 14
s: The two armies set the battle in array in the valley of Zephathah at Mareshah, after Asa's prayer for help. The LORD strikes the Ethiopians, who flee, and Asa's army pursues them to Gerar, where they are destroyed. Judah then plunders the cities around Gerar and returns to Jerusalem with much booty.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 15
s: Azariah the son of Oded, moved by the Spirit of God, meets King Asa and all Judah and Benjamin and tells them that the LORD is with those who seek him, recalling Israel's past distress without the true God, a teaching priest, or law. Encouraged, Asa removes the abominations from Judah and Benjamin and from captured cities in Ephraim, and renews the LORD's altar. In the third month of his fifteenth year, people from Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon gather at Jerusalem, sacrifice seven hundred cattle and seven thousand sheep, and swear a covenant to seek the LORD with all their heart, on pain of death for those who do not. Asa removes his mother Maacah as queen mother for making an abominable image for an Asherah, and destroys the image. The high places remain, but Asa's heart is perfect, he brings dedicated gifts into God's house, and there is no war until his thirty-fifth year.

l: Azariah the son of Oded, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 15
s: Azariah, on whom the Spirit of God came, went out to meet Asa and addressed him and all Judah and Benjamin. He told them the LORD is with those who are with him and can be found by those who seek him, but forsakes those who forsake him, and urged Asa to be strong because his work would be rewarded.

l: Asa, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 15
s: Asa took courage on hearing the prophecy, put away the abominations from Judah, Benjamin, and the cities taken in Ephraim, and renewed the LORD's altar. He led the covenant gathering at Jerusalem in his fifteenth year, removed his mother Maacah as queen mother and destroyed her image, and brought dedicated silver, gold, and vessels into God's house. His heart was perfect all his days, though the high places were not removed.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 15
s: The LORD is described as being with those who are with him, and as being found by those who seek him, as happened when Israel turned to him in distress and when Judah sought him by oath. He troubled the nations with adversity in the earlier times, and he gave Judah rest all around after the covenant.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 15
s: Judah, together with Benjamin, was addressed by Azariah and gathered at Jerusalem under Asa. All Judah rejoiced at the oath, having sworn with all their heart, and the LORD gave them rest, with no war until the thirty-fifth year of Asa's reign.

l: Israel, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 15
s: Azariah recalled that Israel had long been without the true God, a teaching priest, and law, but was found by God when it turned to him in distress. Many people came out of Israel to Asa when they saw the LORD was with him, though the high places were not taken away out of Israel.

l: Maacah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 15
s: Maacah, the mother of King Asa, was removed from being queen mother because she had made an abominable image for an Asherah. Asa cut down her image, ground it into dust, and burned it at the brook Kidron.

l: covenant to seek the LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 15
s: In the third month of Asa's fifteenth year, the assembly at Jerusalem entered a covenant to seek the LORD, the God of their fathers, with all their heart and soul. Anyone who would not seek him was to be put to death, and the people swore it with a loud voice, shouting, trumpets, and cornets, after which the LORD was found by them and gave rest.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 16
s: In the thirty-sixth year of his reign, Asa of Judah faced Baasha of Israel, who built Ramah to block movement in and out of Judah. Asa sent silver and gold from the treasuries of the LORD's house and the king's house to Ben Hadad of Syria, who broke his treaty with Baasha and attacked Israelite cities, so Baasha stopped building Ramah. Asa then carried away Ramah's stones and timber to build Geba and Mizpah. The seer Hanani rebuked Asa for relying on the king of Syria rather than the LORD, and Asa put him in prison and oppressed some of the people. Asa later suffered a severe foot disease, sought only physicians, died in his forty-first year, and was buried in his own tomb in David's city with spices and a great fire.

l: Asa, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 16
s: Asa, king of Judah, paid Ben Hadad with silver and gold from the temple and royal treasuries to break his treaty with Baasha, then used Ramah's stones and timber to build Geba and Mizpah. He was rebuked by Hanani for relying on Syria instead of the LORD, responded by imprisoning the seer and oppressing some people, and was told he would have wars from then on. He was diseased in his feet in his thirty-ninth year, sought only physicians, died in his forty-first year, and was buried in his own tomb in David's city.

l: Baasha, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 16
s: Baasha, king of Israel, went up against Judah and built Ramah to prevent anyone from going out or coming in to Asa. When Ben Hadad's armies struck Israelite cities, he stopped building Ramah and let his work cease.

l: Ben Hadad, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 16
s: Ben Hadad, king of Syria, who lived at Damascus, listened to Asa after receiving silver and gold. He sent his army captains against Israel, who struck Ijon, Dan, Abel Maim, and all the storage cities of Naphtali. Hanani later said the Syrian army had escaped Asa's hand because Asa relied on Syria's king.

l: Hanani, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 16
s: Hanani the seer told Asa that relying on the king of Syria rather than the LORD was foolish, recalled the defeat of the Ethiopians and Lubim through reliance on the LORD, and warned Asa of wars to come. Asa was angry and put him in prison.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 16
s: The LORD's house supplied part of the silver and gold Asa sent to Syria. Hanani said the LORD delivered the huge Ethiopian and Lubim army into Asa's hand when he relied on him, and that his eyes run throughout the earth to show himself strong for those whose heart is perfect toward him. Asa did not seek him in his disease.

l: Ramah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 16
s: Ramah was built by Baasha to block access to Asa's Judah. Building stopped when Ben Hadad attacked Israel's cities, and Asa and Judah carried away its stones and timber to build Geba and Mizpah.

l: treaty between Asa and Ben Hadad, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 16
s: Asa proposed a treaty with Ben Hadad like the one between their fathers, sending silver and gold and asking him to break his treaty with Baasha. Ben Hadad agreed and attacked Israelite cities, which made Baasha withdraw from Ramah, though Hanani condemned Asa's reliance on Syria.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 17
s: Jehoshaphat succeeds his father as king of Judah and strengthens himself against Israel by placing forces and garrisons in Judah's fortified cities and in the cities of Ephraim that Asa had taken. The LORD is with him because he follows the ways of his father David, seeks God, and rejects the Baals and the ways of Israel, so the kingdom is established and Judah brings him tribute, riches, and honor. He removes the high places and Asherah poles and, in his third year, sends princes, Levites, and priests with the book of the LORD's law to teach throughout the cities of Judah. The fear of the LORD falls on surrounding kingdoms, so they make no war on him, and the Philistines and Arabians bring presents and tribute. Jehoshaphat grows great, builds fortresses and store cities, and keeps large armies of mighty men of valor from Judah and Benjamin under named captains.

l: Jehoshaphat, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 17
s: Jehoshaphat becomes king in place of his father, strengthens himself against Israel, and garrisons the fortified cities of Judah and the cities of Ephraim that Asa had taken. He walks in the first ways of David, seeks the God of his father, rejects the Baals, and removes the high places and Asherah poles. He sends teachers throughout Judah, receives tribute and presents, grows exceedingly great, builds fortresses and store cities, and commands vast numbers of mighty men of valor.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 17
s: The LORD is with Jehoshaphat because he seeks God and walks in His commandments, and He establishes the kingdom in his hand. The fear of the LORD falls on all the surrounding kingdoms so that they make no war against Jehoshaphat. His law is carried in a book through the cities of Judah.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 17
s: Judah's fortified cities receive forces and garrisons, and all Judah brings tribute to Jehoshaphat. The high places and Asherah poles are removed from it, and its cities are taught from the book of the LORD's law. Jehoshaphat builds fortresses and store cities there, and three of the army captains are listed as coming from Judah, commanding 300,000, 280,000, and 200,000 men.

l: princes (Jehoshaphat's princes), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 17
s: In the third year of Jehoshaphat's reign, he sends his princes Ben Hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah to teach in the cities of Judah. They go accompanied by Levites and priests.

l: Levites, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 17
s: Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tobadonijah, the Levites, are sent with the princes to teach in Judah's cities. The priests Elishama and Jehoram go with them, and together they carry the book of the LORD's law among the people.

l: teaching mission, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 17
s: In the third year of his reign, Jehoshaphat sends princes, Levites, and priests to teach in the cities of Judah. They carry the book of the LORD's law and go throughout all the cities, teaching among the people.

l: army of mighty men of valor, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 17
s: Jehoshaphat keeps mighty men of valor in Jerusalem, numbered by fathers' houses under captains. From Judah, Adnah commands 300,000, Jehohanan 280,000, and Amasiah son of Zichri, who willingly offered himself to the LORD, 200,000. From Benjamin, Eliada commands 200,000 armed with bow and shield, and Jehozabad 180,000 ready for war; these wait on the king, in addition to those placed in the fortified cities.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 18
s: Jehoshaphat of Judah, allied with Ahab of Israel, visits Samaria and agrees to join Ahab in war against Ramoth Gilead, but insists on first inquiring of the LORD. Ahab's four hundred prophets, with Zedekiah's iron horns, promise victory, while Micaiah, whom Ahab hates, first echoes them sarcastically and then reports a vision of Israel scattered and of a lying spirit sent into the prophets' mouths. Zedekiah strikes Micaiah, and Ahab orders him imprisoned on bread and water until Ahab returns in peace. Ahab disguises himself in battle, but a randomly shot arrow wounds him and he dies at sunset, while Jehoshaphat, mistaken for Ahab by the Syrian chariot captains, is saved when he cries out and the LORD helps him.

l: Jehoshaphat, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 18
s: Jehoshaphat, rich and honored, allied himself with Ahab and went to Samaria, pledging his people to join the war on Ramoth Gilead. He insisted on inquiring for the LORD's word and asked for a true prophet of the LORD, rebuking Ahab's dismissal of Micaiah. In battle, wearing his royal robes at Ahab's urging, he was mistaken for Ahab by the Syrian chariot captains, cried out, and was saved when the LORD helped him and moved them away.

l: Ahab, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 18
s: Ahab, king of Israel, feasted Jehoshaphat and persuaded him to go with him to Ramoth Gilead. He trusted his four hundred prophets, said he hated Micaiah for never prophesying good about him, and had him imprisoned on bread and water after hearing a prophecy of evil. He disguised himself in battle, was struck by a randomly shot arrow between the joints of his armor, propped himself up in his chariot until evening, and died at about sunset.

l: Micaiah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 18
s: Micaiah son of Imla was the one prophet Ahab hated for always speaking evil about him. Warned to match the other prophets, he swore to say only what God says; he first told Ahab to go up and prosper, then, when adjured to tell the truth, described Israel scattered like shepherdless sheep and a vision of the LORD sending a lying spirit into the prophets. He was struck by Zedekiah and ordered imprisoned, and he answered that if Ahab returned in peace the LORD had not spoken by him.

l: Zedekiah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 18
s: Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made iron horns and prophesied in the LORD's name that Ahab would push the Syrians until they were consumed. He struck Micaiah on the cheek and sarcastically asked which way the LORD's Spirit went from him. Micaiah replied that Zedekiah would see on that day when he went into an inner room to hide.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 18
s: The LORD is described by Micaiah as sitting on his throne with the army of heaven around him and asking who would entice Ahab to fall at Ramoth Gilead.
