He accepted a spirit's offer to be a lying spirit in the mouth of Ahab's prophets and sent it, speaking evil against Ahab. He also helped Jehoshaphat when he cried out, moving the Syrian captains to leave him.

l: Ramoth Gilead, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 18
s: Ramoth Gilead is the place Ahab and Jehoshaphat decide to go to in battle against the Syrians, after Ahab's prophets promise God will deliver it into the king's hand. It is where Micaiah says Ahab will fall, and where Ahab is fatally wounded.

l: captains of the chariots (king of Syria's), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 18
s: The captains of the Syrian king's chariots had been ordered to fight only the king of Israel, not small or great. They mistook Jehoshaphat for Ahab and turned to attack him, then turned back from pursuing him when they saw he was not the king of Israel.

l: prophets (Ahab's four hundred), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 18
s: Ahab's four hundred prophets, gathered at the gate of Samaria, all prophesied with one mouth that the king should go up to Ramoth Gilead and prosper because the LORD would deliver it to him. According to Micaiah, the LORD had put a lying spirit in their mouths, and the outcome showed their word to be false.

l: lying spirit, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 18
s: A spirit came out and stood before the LORD, volunteering to entice Ahab by being a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets. The LORD told it that it would entice him and prevail, and to go and do so, according to Micaiah's account.

l: battle at Ramoth Gilead, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 18
s: Ahab and Jehoshaphat went up to the battle, with Ahab disguised and Jehoshaphat in his robes. The Syrian chariot captains went after Jehoshaphat by mistake until he was delivered, and a random arrow wounded Ahab. The battle increased that day, and Ahab died at about sunset.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 19
s: Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, returns in peace to Jerusalem, where Jehu the son of Hanani the seer confronts him for helping the wicked and loving those who hate the LORD, warning that wrath is on him, yet acknowledging the good in him for removing the Asheroth and seeking God. Jehoshaphat then goes among the people from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim and brings them back to the LORD. He sets judges in all the fortified cities of Judah and charges them to judge for the LORD, in fear of him, without iniquity, partiality, or bribes. In Jerusalem he appoints Levites, priests, and heads of fathers' households to give judgment for the LORD and settle controversies, instructing them to warn people against guilt toward the LORD. He names Amariah the chief priest over the matters of the LORD and Zebadiah the son of Ishmael over the king's matters, and tells them to deal courageously.

l: Jehoshaphat, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 19
s: Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, returned in peace to Jerusalem and was rebuked by Jehu for helping the wicked, though Jehu noted he had removed the Asheroth and set his heart to seek God. He went among the people from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim and brought them back to the LORD, then appointed judges in Judah's fortified cities and Levites, priests, and family heads in Jerusalem, charging them to act in the fear of the LORD.

l: Jehu the son of Hanani the seer, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 19
s: Jehu the seer went out to meet King Jehoshaphat and asked whether he should help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD, declaring that wrath from the LORD was on him. He also said good things were found in Jehoshaphat, because he had put away the Asheroth and set his heart to seek God.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 19
s: The LORD is said to have wrath against Jehoshaphat for helping the wicked, yet good is found in the king for seeking God. He is called the God of the fathers of the people, and judges are told they judge for him and that he is with them in judgment. There is no iniquity with him, nor respect of persons, nor taking of bribes, and the text hopes he will be with the good.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 19
s: Judah is the land of King Jehoshaphat, from which the Asheroth had been put away. Judges were set throughout all its fortified cities, city by city, and Zebadiah the son of Ishmael is named ruler of the house of Judah in all the king's matters.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 19
s: Jerusalem is where Jehoshaphat returned in peace, where he lived, and where Jehu met him. There he appointed certain Levites, priests, and heads of fathers' households to give judgment for the LORD and for controversies, and the controversies of brothers in their cities were to come to them.

l: judges (Jehoshaphat's judges in the fortified cities of Judah), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 19
s: Jehoshaphat set these judges in all the fortified cities of Judah, city by city. He told them to consider what they do, since they judge not for man but for the LORD, who is with them in judgment, and to let the fear of the LORD be on them, with no iniquity, partiality, or bribes.

l: people of Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 19
s: Jehoshaphat went out among the people from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim and brought them back to the LORD, the God of their fathers. Their controversies, between blood and blood, law and commandment, statutes and ordinances, were to be brought to the appointed judges in Jerusalem, who were to warn them against guilt toward the LORD.

l: judgment and justice, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 19
s: Judgment is presented as being done for the LORD, in his fear, faithfully and with a perfect heart, free of iniquity, respect of persons, and bribes. Those judging controversies must warn people not to be guilty toward the LORD so that wrath does not come on them and their brothers, and are told to deal courageously, with Amariah the chief priest over the LORD's matters and Levites serving as officers.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 20
s: Moab, Ammon, and some Meunites come against King Jehoshaphat of Judah, and he responds by proclaiming a fast and praying before the assembly in the LORD's house, admitting Judah has no might and that their eyes are on God. The Levite Jahaziel, moved by the LORD's Spirit, tells them the battle is God's and that they need only stand still and watch. Judah goes out with Levites singing praise at the front, and the LORD sets ambushers so that Ammon and Moab destroy the people of Mount Seir and then each other. Judah gathers plunder for three days, blesses the LORD in Beracah Valley, and returns to Jerusalem rejoicing, and the surrounding kingdoms fear God. The chapter closes with a summary of Jehoshaphat's reign and his alliance with Ahaziah king of Israel to build ships, which the LORD destroys after Eliezer prophesies against him.

l: Jehoshaphat, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 20
s: Jehoshaphat is alarmed by the coming multitude, proclaims a fast, and prays before the assembly, then urges the people to believe the LORD and his prophets and appoints singers to go before the army. After the victory he leads Judah back to Jerusalem with joy and enjoys rest on all sides. His reign of twenty-five years began at thirty-five; he walked in Asa's way, though the high places remained, and he later joined Ahaziah in a ship venture that the LORD wrecked after Eliezer's rebuke.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 20
s: The LORD is addressed by Jehoshaphat as ruler over all the nations, and he answers through Jahaziel that the battle is his and Judah need only stand still. When the singing begins he sets ambushers against the enemy, bringing about their destruction, and gives Jehoshaphat's realm rest. He later destroys Jehoshaphat's ships because of the alliance with Ahaziah.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 20
s: Judah gathers from all its cities to seek the LORD, stands before him with wives and children, and worships after hearing the promise of deliverance. They go out without needing to fight, collect plunder for three days, bless the LORD in Beracah Valley, and return to Jerusalem with instruments and joy.

l: Moab, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 20
s: The children of Moab, with Ammon and some Meunites, come against Jehoshaphat to battle. Jehoshaphat notes that Israel had spared them when leaving Egypt. Moab and Ammon rise against the inhabitants of Mount Seir to destroy them, then help destroy one another.

l: Ammon, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 20
s: The children of Ammon join Moab in coming against Judah, and Jehoshaphat laments that they repay Israel's earlier mercy. Ammon and Moab attack and destroy Mount Seir's inhabitants, then turn on each other until none escape.

l: Mount Seir, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 20
s: The inhabitants of Mount Seir are named among those who came against Judah. The LORD's ambushers strike them, and Ammon and Moab rise up to kill and destroy them utterly.

l: Jahaziel, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 20
s: Jahaziel is a Levite of the sons of Asaph, son of Zechariah, upon whom the LORD's Spirit comes in the middle of the assembly. He tells Judah not to fear because the battle is God's, directs them to go down the next day, and says they will not need to fight.

l: invasion of Judah by Moab, Ammon and Mount Seir, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 20
s: A great multitude of Moab, Ammon, and Meunites is reported at Hazazon Tamar (En Gedi), prompting Judah's fast and prayer. The invaders are destroyed without Judah fighting, as the LORD sets ambushers and the enemy forces turn on each other. Judah finds only dead bodies and spends three days taking plunder.

l: praise and singing, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 20
s: The Levites of the Kohathites and Korahites praise the LORD with an exceedingly loud voice, and Jehoshaphat appoints singers in holy array to go before the army saying, "Give thanks to the LORD, for his loving kindness endures forever." When they began to sing and praise, the LORD set ambushers against the enemy. Judah later returns to Jerusalem with stringed instruments, harps, and trumpets.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 21
s: Jehoshaphat dies and his firstborn son Jehoram becomes king of Judah, then kills his brothers and some princes of Israel. Following the ways of Ahab's house, to which he is tied by marriage, he does evil and leads Judah into idolatry, while the LORD spares David's house because of his covenant. Edom and Libnah revolt, and Elijah sends a letter announcing a plague and a fatal bowel disease. The Philistines and Arabians raid Judah and carry off the king's possessions, sons, and wives, leaving only Jehoahaz, and Jehoram dies of the disease after two years, unmourned and not buried in the kings' tombs.

l: Jehoram, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 21
s: Jehoram, Jehoshaphat's firstborn, became king at thirty-two and reigned eight years in Jerusalem. After strengthening himself he killed all his brothers and some princes of Israel, walked in the ways of Ahab's house (his wife was Ahab's daughter), built high places, and led Judah astray. He lost Edom and Libnah, saw his sons and wives carried off, died of an incurable bowel disease, and was buried in David's city but not in the kings' tombs.

l: Jehoshaphat, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 21
s: Jehoshaphat died and was buried with his fathers in David's city, and his son Jehoram reigned in his place. He had given his other sons great gifts and fortified cities, but gave the kingdom to Jehoram as the firstborn. Elijah's letter later cites his ways as a standard Jehoram failed to follow.

l: Jehoshaphat's sons (Jehoram's brothers), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 21
s: Six sons of Jehoshaphat are named besides Jehoram: Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah. Their father gave them silver, gold, precious things, and fortified cities in Judah. Jehoram killed them all with the sword, and Elijah's letter says they were better than he was.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 21
s: The LORD did not destroy David's house because of his covenant with David and his promise of a lamp to him and his children. He judged Jehoram by letting Edom and Libnah revolt, stirring up the Philistines and Arabians against him, and striking him with an incurable bowel disease.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 21
s: Judah was led astray by Jehoram, who made high places in its mountains and made Jerusalem's inhabitants play the prostitute. Edom revolted from its control, as did Libnah. The Philistines and Arabians then invaded, broke in, and carried off the possessions in the king's house.

l: Edom, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 21
s: Edom revolted from Judah's rule in Jehoram's days and made a king over itself. Jehoram went there with his captains and chariots and struck the Edomites who surrounded him by night, yet Edom has remained in revolt to this day.

l: Elijah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 21
s: Elijah the prophet sent Jehoram a letter delivering the LORD's word of judgment. It condemned him for not following Jehoshaphat and Asa, for following the kings of Israel, and for killing his brothers.

l: letter (Elijah's letter), The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 21
s: The letter from Elijah came to Jehoram in the name of the LORD, the God of David. It charged him with walking in Israel's kings' ways, leading Judah into prostitution, and slaying his better brothers. It foretold a great plague on his people, children, wives, and possessions, and a bowel disease that would make his bowels fall out.

l: Philistines, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 21
s: The LORD stirred up the spirit of the Philistines against Jehoram. They came up with the Arabians, broke into Judah, and carried away the possessions in the king's house, along with his sons and wives.

l: Arabians, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 21
s: The Arabians, who live beside the Ethiopians, were stirred up by the LORD against Jehoram. With the Philistines they invaded Judah and carried off the king's possessions, sons, and wives, leaving only Jehoahaz, the youngest son.

l: Jehoram's illness, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 21
s: After the invasion the LORD struck Jehoram in his bowels with an incurable disease, as Elijah's letter had foretold. After two years his bowels fell out and he died of severe diseases. His people made no burning for him as for his fathers, and he departed with no one's regret.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 22
s: The inhabitants of Jerusalem make Ahaziah, the youngest son of Jehoram, king of Judah after raiders have slain his older brothers. Ahaziah follows the wicked counsel of Ahab's house, including his mother Athaliah, and goes with Jehoram of Israel to war against Hazael of Syria, where Joram is wounded. While visiting the wounded Jehoram in Jezreel, Ahaziah is caught by Jehu, whom the LORD had anointed to cut off Ahab's house, and is killed, though he is buried because of his father Jehoshaphat's faithfulness. Athaliah then destroys all the royal offspring of Judah, but Jehoshabeath, wife of Jehoiada the priest, hides Joash in God's house, where he remains six years while Athaliah reigns.

l: Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 22
s: Ahaziah was made king by the inhabitants of Jerusalem at forty-two years old and reigned one year, walking in the evil ways of Ahab's house under his mother's counsel. He joined Jehoram of Israel against Hazael of Syria, visited the wounded Jehoram in Jezreel, and his destruction was of God. He was caught hiding in Samaria, brought to Jehu, killed, and buried because he was the son of Jehoshaphat.

l: Athaliah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 22
s: Athaliah, daughter of Omri, was Ahaziah's mother and his counselor in acting wickedly. When she saw her son was dead, she destroyed all the royal offspring of the house of Judah and then reigned over the land for six years.

l: house of Ahab, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 22
s: Ahab's house served as counselors to Ahaziah after his father's death, leading him to evil and to his destruction. Jehu, anointed by the LORD, was executing judgment on it and cutting it off.

l: Jehu the son of Nimshi, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 22
s: Jehu is identified as the one whom the LORD had anointed to cut off Ahab's house. While executing judgment on it, he found and killed the princes of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah's brothers who served Ahaziah, and Ahaziah was brought to him and killed.

l: Jehoshabeath, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 22
s: Jehoshabeath, the king's daughter, was the daughter of King Jehoram, sister of Ahaziah, and wife of Jehoiada the priest. She stealthily rescued Joash from among the slain king's sons and hid him with his nurse in the bedroom so Athaliah could not kill him.

l: Joash, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 22
s: Joash was rescued by Jehoshabeath from among the king's sons who were being slain. He was hidden with his nurse, first in the bedroom and then in God's house, for six years while Athaliah reigned.

l: royal offspring of the house of Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 22
s: Athaliah destroyed all the royal offspring of the house of Judah after her son Ahaziah died. Joash alone was rescued from among the king's sons who were slain.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 23
s: In the seventh year, the priest Jehoiada made a covenant with five captains of hundreds, gathered the Levites and the heads of Israel's households to Jerusalem, and organized them to guard the LORD's house and the king's son. They armed the people with David's spears and shields, crowned the king's son, gave him the covenant, anointed him, and proclaimed 'Long live the king!' When Athaliah heard the noise, came to the LORD's house, and cried 'Treason!', Jehoiada ordered her taken out between the ranks and killed outside the house, and she was slain at the horse gate. Jehoiada then made a covenant that the people would be the LORD's people, and the people destroyed Baal's house and killed Mattan the priest of Baal. Jehoiada restored the temple order of priests, Levites, offerings, and gatekeepers, and the king was set on the throne, with the people rejoicing and the city quiet.

l: Jehoiada, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 23
s: Jehoiada the priest strengthened himself in the seventh year, made a covenant with the captains of hundreds, and directed the Levites and people in guarding the king's son and the temple. He had the king crowned and anointed with his sons, ordered Athaliah removed and killed outside the LORD's house, and made a covenant between himself, the people, and the king. He then destroyed Baal worship's presence, restored the temple's offerings and gatekeepers, and brought the king to the throne.

l: Athaliah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 23
s: Athaliah heard the noise of the people praising the king and came into the LORD's house, where she saw the king standing by his pillar and tore her clothes, crying 'Treason! treason!' Jehoiada ordered her brought out between the ranks and not killed in the LORD's house. She was killed at the entrance of the horse gate to the king's house.

l: Joash, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 23
s: The king's son was brought out, crowned, given the covenant, made king, and anointed by Jehoiada and his sons, while the people cried 'Long live the king!' He stood by his pillar at the entrance amid captains, trumpeters, and rejoicing people, and was guarded by the Levites. He was then brought down from the LORD's house through the upper gate and set on the throne of the kingdom.

l: captains of hundreds, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 23
s: Five captains of hundreds were named: Azariah son of Jeroham, Ishmael son of Jehohanan, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat son of Zichri, and Jehoiada took them into covenant with him. Jehoiada gave them David's spears, bucklers, and shields, and later directed them to bring Athaliah out between the ranks. They also helped bring the king down to his house and set him on the throne.

l: Levites, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 23
s: The Levites were gathered from all the cities of Judah to Jerusalem, and were assigned with the priests as gatekeepers in three groups. They were told to surround the king, each with weapons in hand, to kill anyone entering the house, and to stay with the king. They did all that Jehoiada commanded, with the incoming and outgoing Sabbath shifts both kept on duty.

l: people of Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 23
s: The people of Judah, with the heads of fathers' households, came to Jerusalem and made a covenant with the king in God's house. They stood in the courts with weapons around the king, rejoiced and blew trumpets at his crowning, and broke down the house of Baal, its altars and images, and killed Mattan its priest. They rejoiced after Athaliah's death, and the city was quiet.

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 23
s: The LORD is invoked as having spoken that the king's son must reign according to his promise concerning the sons of David. The people are made a covenant that they should be the LORD's people, and the temple offerings are restored to be made to him as written in the law of Moses. Athaliah is not to be killed in his house, and no one unclean may enter it.

l: the LORD's house, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 23
s: The LORD's house is the site where the covenant with the king was made, where only priests and ministering Levites were permitted to enter, and where David's weapons were kept. The king was crowned there, and Athaliah was taken out of it before being killed. Jehoiada appointed officers over it for burnt offerings and set gatekeepers so no unclean person could enter.

l: covenant, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 23
s: A covenant appears at several stages: Jehoiada's covenant with the captains of hundreds, the assembly's covenant with the king in God's house, and the covenant given to the king at his crowning. Jehoiada then made a covenant between himself, all the people, and the king that they should be the LORD's people.

l: coronation of the king, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 23
s: The king's son was brought out, crowned, given the covenant, made king, and anointed by Jehoiada and his sons, with the people saying 'Long live the king!' The people rejoiced, trumpeters stood by the king, and singers led praise with instruments. Later he was set on the throne of the kingdom.

l: killing of Athaliah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 23
s: After Athaliah cried 'Treason!', Jehoiada ordered her brought out between the ranks, with anyone following her to be slain, and insisted she not be killed in the LORD's house. She was made way for, went to the entrance of the horse gate to the king's house, and was killed there. Afterward the people rejoiced and the city was quiet.

l: The Second Book of Chronicles, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 24
s: Joash became king of Judah at age seven and did right while the priest Jehoiada lived. He ordered the repair of the LORD's house, which had been damaged by the sons of Athaliah, and when the Levites were slow he had a chest set at the temple gate to collect Moses' tax; the people gave abundantly, workmen restored the house, and leftover money made vessels. After Jehoiada died at 130 and was buried among the kings, the princes of Judah persuaded Joash to abandon the LORD for Asherah poles and idols. Zechariah, Jehoiada's son, rebuked the people and was stoned at the king's command, after which a small Syrian army defeated Judah, wounded Joash, and his own servants Zabad and Jehozabad killed him in his bed, and Amaziah his son succeeded him.

l: Joash, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 24
s: Joash began to reign at seven and reigned forty years in Jerusalem, doing right all the days of Jehoiada. He commissioned the temple repair, but after Jehoiada's death he listened to the princes, abandoned the LORD, and ordered Zechariah killed. The Syrians wounded him, his servants killed him on his bed, and he was buried in David's city but not in the kings' tombs; Amaziah his son reigned after him.

l: Jehoiada, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 24
s: Jehoiada the priest, called the chief, guided Joash, took two wives for him, and with the king oversaw the money used to restore the LORD's house. He died full of days at 130 and was buried in David's city among the kings for his good toward Israel, God, and his house. His son Zechariah was later killed by Joash, and Joash's servants killed the king for the blood of Jehoiada's sons.

l: Zechariah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 24
s: Zechariah, son of Jehoiada the priest, was moved by the Spirit of God to stand above the people and warn that forsaking the LORD meant being forsaken. The people conspired against him and stoned him in the court of the LORD's house at the king's command. As he died he said, "May the LORD look at it, and repay it."

l: LORD, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 24
s: The LORD's house was repaired through the people's gifts, and the LORD sent prophets to call Judah back after it abandoned him. Because Judah forsook him, wrath came on Judah and Jerusalem, and he delivered a very great army into the hands of the small Syrian force, executing judgment on Joash.

l: Jerusalem, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 24
s: Jerusalem was where Joash reigned forty years and where the proclamation to bring the tax went out. Wrath came on it for the idolatry after Jehoiada's death, and the Syrians came against it and destroyed the princes of the people. Jehoiada and Joash were both buried in David's city.

l: Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 24
s: Judah's cities were the places from which money was to be gathered for the temple repair, and its people gladly gave to the chest. After Jehoiada died, Judah's princes led it into serving Asherah poles and idols, so wrath came on it. The Syrians then came up against Judah and destroyed its princes.

l: the LORD's house, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 24
s: The LORD's house had been broken up by the sons of Athaliah, who gave its dedicated things to the Baals. Joash had it restored with masons, carpenters, and iron and bronze workers, set up as designed and strengthened, and vessels were made from the leftover money. Burnt offerings were offered there continually during Jehoiada's life, but the princes and people later abandoned it, and Zechariah was stoned in its court.

l: priests and Levites, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 24
s: Joash gathered the priests and Levites and told them to collect money from the cities of Judah to repair the house, but the Levites did not act right away. Later Levites carried the chest to the king's officers when it was full.

l: Syrians, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 24
s: The Syrian army came up against Judah and Jerusalem at the end of the year with a small company, destroyed the princes of the people, and sent the plunder to the king of Damascus. The LORD gave them victory over a very great army because Judah had forsaken him, and they left Joash seriously wounded.

l: princes of Judah, The Second Book of Chronicles, Chapter 24
s: After Jehoiada's death the princes of Judah bowed down to Joash, and he listened to them, leading to the abandonment of the LORD's house and service of Asherah poles and idols. Earlier they had rejoiced and given to the chest, and later the Syrians destroyed them.
